verdicts.trueWording: that’s what Wolfe himself said in “Words Weird and Wonderful.”
verdicts.note: Line reads: 'That’s what all the fans were saying, that the words were real, and then that’s what Wolfe himself said in “Words Weird and Wonderful.”' The interviewer's preceding question supplies 'real words and not Wolfe’s coinages'; the article is placed in The Castle of the Otter. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: How soon did you uncover the various naming schemes Wolfe uses… like naming people in the Commonwealth after Catholic saints?
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Andre-Driussi speaks the quoted words — they are the interviewer Master Ultan's question, not Andre-Driussi's speech
verdicts.note: The quoted string is verbatim but sits inside Master Ultan's question. Andre-Driussi's own reply endorses the substance ('The saints clue was given in Castle. Still, nobody had published the results of tracking them all down') and adds further group schemes he found himself — 'the “iron” names of the sailors, the star names of the people in Yesod' — so the naming-schemes-by-group substance holds; only the attribution of the wording fails.

verdicts.trueWording: who sometimes wrote them as he heard them but more often translated them when he understood… their meanings
verdicts.note: Wowra introduces the block quote as from 'the Foreword to Soldier of the Mist' with the citation '(Soldier of the Mist, 1986, xii)'. Byline 'By Scott Wowra', dated 'On 7 September 2016'. Wolfe's translator persona says 'I have followed the original writer, who sometimes wrote them...' — the original writer being Latro, the narrator. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: This process of translation is referred to as folk etymology, and it is the primary method Latro uses to record his place names.
verdicts.note: Verbatim in Wowra's own voice, immediately after the Foreword quotation. Latro is the narrator of Soldier of the Mist.

verdicts.trueWording: classify… according to Stewart’s taxonomy. The predominant category is folk etymology
verdicts.note: Full sentence: 'The following sections attempt to classify some of Latro’s place names in Soldier of the Mist according to Stewart’s taxonomy. The predominant category is folk etymology, followed by the less frequent use of descriptive, associative, and commemorative place names.' The toponymic-taxonomy limb is George Stewart's (1975) taxonomy, named on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: these include folk etymology, association, description, and commemoration
verdicts.note: Verbatim. Page: 'Latro uses a variety of methods to generate place names and, applying the categories provided by academic toponomy, we can identify that these include folk etymology, association, description, and commemoration.' Note the page's hedge is 'include' rather than an explicit 'four', but the essay's own summary enumerates exactly these four ('folk etymology, followed by the less frequent use of descriptive, associative, and commemorative place names') and its section structure follows them, so the four-process limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Silent Country | Laconia | Gk. Lakōnikos – taciturn (Spartans were renowned for brevity in speech)
verdicts.note: The quote is a cell in Wowra's Folk Etymology table, on the row whose first two columns are 'Silent Country' (Latro's name) and 'Laconia' (English place name). Corroborated in the essay body, where Wolfe's introduction is quoted: 'Latro seems to have heard some taciturn person referred to as having Laconic manners, and to have concluded that Laconia meant “Silent Country.”'

verdicts.trueWording: Latro calls Athens Thought because that’s what he thinks it means. As it turns out, he’s right.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and the attribution holds: Wowra introduces the block quote as from 'Darrell Schweitzer’s interview with Mr. Wolfe that appeared in the Spring 1988 edition of Weird Tales', and the reference list carries 'Schweitzer, D. (1988). “Profile: Gene Wolfe”. Spring 1988 issue of Weird Tales'. Latro is the narrator.

verdicts.trueWording: most importantly, he doesn’t tell certain things to the reader straight away
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the blogger's numbered response to reason 1. The post is explicitly a reread ('When I started rereading it, I intended to review only The Shadow of the Torturer').

verdicts.trueWording: Even though Severian is an unreliable narrator strictu sensu, as far as I can tell, he doesn’t lie to the reader.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the essay disputes a 'common claim that Severian lies to the reader' — the received view it answers is 'Severian is an unreliable narrator', and three paragraphs later the same essay asserts the opposite of the claim's holding
verdicts.note: The quoted words are verbatim and are the blogger's own qualified position ('as far as I can tell'). But the page never frames 'Severian lies to the reader' as the common claim; the alleged difficulty it lists is '1) Severian is an unreliable narrator'. More sharply, the same essay soon states 'We know that Severian is a liar quite early on' and reasons from 'Severian’s lies' and 'what intent may be behind Severian’s lies', so 'holding that he does not' is not a position the essay sustains. Anyone reusing this must not present the essay as settled on the point.

verdicts.trueWording: the book reportedly being a found text… and because of that had to resort to obscure words to use for animals and things that do not exist yet
verdicts.note: Verbatim, as item 3 of the essay's list 'Interpreting TBotNS is allegedly difficult for a couple of reasons'. The causal limb is explicit ('because of that'), and the found-text conceit is stated ('as Wolfe claims he has translated it from the original future language'). The 'allegedly' hedges whether these reasons make interpretation difficult, not the found-text mechanism; the blogger's own reply to reason 3 accepts the obscure words and only denies they impede enjoyment.

verdicts.trueWording: he describes his world in a way that an actual character of this world would describe it: to the best of their knowledge
verdicts.note: Verbatim. Post bylined 'Noel', dated June 3, 2015, and self-described as by a fiction writer ('So where does that leave a fiction writer like me?'). 'Actual character of this world' supports 'actual inhabitant of that world'.

verdicts.trueWording: strange creatures inhabit this world and yet we only get the barest of descriptions as to their nature
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the same sentence chain as the light-fishes and aliens examples.

verdicts.trueWording: To me, the most interesting stories arise from the untold details.
No, don’t tell me histories as if they were written in books. Tell me histories that arise from your psyche. Tell me histories that surface from interaction with your surroundings.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the wanted history surfaces from a character's interaction with surroundings — the page addresses the writer ('your psyche', 'your surroundings'), never a character
verdicts.note: The rejection limb is verbatim. The positive half is addressed in the second person to the author throughout that paragraph ('your deliberate attempts to flesh out your world', 'your psyche', 'your surroundings'), so the claim's substitution of a character as the agent of the interaction is the claim's inference, not the page's wording.
